title: Healthcare & Medical Privacy Security Checklist
metaDescription: Complete checklist to protect your medical data, ensure HIPAA compliance, and secure health apps from privacy risks and data brokers.
intro: Protect your most sensitive information with this comprehensive healthcare privacy checklist. Learn to secure health apps, understand HIPAA protections, and prevent medical data brokers from accessing your personal health information.

items.task: Audit all health and fitness apps on your devices
items.why: Many health apps share data with third parties, including period trackers that sell reproductive health data to advertisers and data brokers.
items.howTo: Review your phone's app list for health, fitness, period tracking, and wellness apps. Check each app's privacy policy to see what data they collect and share. Delete apps that sell data or have poor privacy practices.

items.task: Restrict health app permissions and data access
items.why: Apps often request excessive permissions to access location, contacts, and other sensitive data beyond what's needed for functionality.
items.howTo: Go to Settings > Privacy on iOS or Settings > Apps & Permissions on Android. Review each health app's permissions and disable location, microphone, camera, and contacts access unless absolutely necessary.

items.task: Disable health data sharing with third parties
items.why: Health apps may share your data with insurance companies, employers, or marketing firms, potentially affecting coverage or employment.
items.howTo: In each health app's settings, look for 'Data Sharing,' 'Third Party Access,' or 'Partners' sections. Disable all data sharing options. Also check Apple Health or Google Fit for connected apps and remove unnecessary connections.

items.task: Switch to privacy-focused period tracking apps
items.why: Popular period trackers like Flo and Clue have been caught sharing intimate reproductive health data with Facebook and other third parties.
items.howTo: Delete period trackers with poor privacy practices. Switch to privacy-focused alternatives like Euki or Drip that don't require accounts and store data locally on your device only.

items.why: Fitness trackers collect detailed health metrics and location data that can reveal medical conditions and daily routines to third parties.
items.howTo: In your fitness tracker app, disable data sharing with third parties, turn off social features, and set health metrics to private. Disable automatic data syncing to employer wellness programs.

items.task: Secure mental health and therapy apps
items.why: Mental health apps often aren't HIPAA-compliant and may share sensitive therapy notes and mental health data with advertisers.
items.howTo: Choose HIPAA-compliant mental health apps when possible. Enable two-factor authentication, use a strong unique password, and disable data sharing. Consider using apps that offer local data storage only.

sections.title: HIPAA Rights and Healthcare Provider Security

items.task: Learn your HIPAA privacy rights and protections
items.why: Understanding HIPAA helps you know when your medical privacy is being violated and what protections you have against unauthorized disclosure.
items.howTo: Request a copy of your healthcare provider's Notice of Privacy Practices. Know your rights to access medical records, request amendments, and file complaints. Understand that HIPAA doesn't cover most health apps or employers.

items.task: Secure your online medical records and patient portals
items.why: Patient portals contain complete medical histories and are prime targets for hackers and identity thieves seeking valuable health data.
items.howTo: Enable two-factor authentication on all patient portal accounts. Use unique, strong passwords for each healthcare provider. Log out completely after each session and never access portals on public Wi-Fi.

items.task: Control medical data sharing between providers
items.why: Healthcare providers may share your data with business associates or third parties without clear disclosure, expanding who has access to your medical information.
items.howTo: Ask your doctor about their data sharing practices. Request to opt out of non-essential data sharing. Review and limit Health Information Exchange (HIE) participation if not needed for your care.

items.task: Protect privacy with health insurance companies
items.why: Insurance companies may use health data for non-coverage purposes like marketing or sell data to third parties including pharmaceutical companies.
items.howTo: Review your insurance company's privacy policy and opt out of data sharing for marketing. Avoid insurance wellness programs that require extensive health data sharing. Consider paying cash for sensitive treatments to keep them off insurance records.

items.task: Secure medical billing and payment information
items.why: Medical billing systems are frequent targets for cybercriminals and contain both financial and health information in one place.
items.howTo: Use secure payment methods for medical bills. Monitor medical billing statements for errors or fraud. Set up account alerts for billing activity and report suspicious charges immediately.

items.task: Use secure telehealth platforms and settings
items.why: Not all telehealth platforms are HIPAA-compliant, and video calls can be intercepted or recorded without proper security measures.
items.howTo: Verify your telehealth platform is HIPAA-compliant. Use waiting rooms and passwords for video appointments. Ensure calls are end-to-end encrypted and disable automatic recording features.

items.task: Secure your internet connection for telehealth
items.why: Public Wi-Fi and unsecured networks can expose your telehealth conversations and medical discussions to eavesdroppers and hackers.
items.howTo: Never use public Wi-Fi for telehealth appointments. Use a VPN like a privacy-focused browser's built-in VPN for additional encryption. Ensure your home Wi-Fi uses WPA3 security and has a strong password.

items.task: Secure devices used for telehealth appointments
items.why: Unsecured devices can be compromised, allowing unauthorized access to your telehealth sessions and stored health information.
items.howTo: Keep devices updated with latest security patches. Use device lock screens with PINs or biometrics. Close other applications during telehealth calls and clear browser cache/history afterward.

items.task: Create a private environment for telehealth calls
items.why: Telehealth conversations can be overheard by family, roommates, or neighbors, compromising your medical privacy and confidentiality.
items.howTo: Use a private room with closed doors for telehealth appointments. Use headphones to prevent others from hearing your conversation. Inform household members not to interrupt during scheduled appointments.

items.task: Secure online pharmacy and prescription apps
items.why: Prescription apps contain detailed medication histories that reveal health conditions and can be valuable targets for identity theft and fraud.
items.howTo: Use two-factor authentication on pharmacy apps. Choose pharmacies with strong privacy policies. Avoid uploading prescription photos to unsecured apps or cloud storage services.

items.task: Use secure channels for health-related communications
items.why: Regular email and text messages about health matters aren't encrypted and can be accessed by third parties or intercepted during transmission.
items.howTo: Use patient portals for communicating with healthcare providers instead of regular email. For urgent communications, use encrypted messaging apps. Avoid discussing sensitive health information via regular SMS or social media.

pro_tips: Use a privacy-focused browser when researching health conditions online to prevent health-related searches from being tracked and used for targeted advertising.
Pay cash for sensitive medical treatments or prescriptions to keep them off insurance records and reduce data trail exposure.
Regularly search for your name plus health-related terms to check if your medical information has been exposed in data breaches or by data brokers.
Create a separate email address specifically for health-related accounts to contain potential data breaches and make monitoring easier.
Consider using a pseudonym for non-critical health apps and services that don't require legal identification for additional privacy protection.
